name: Priya Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making the time, Priya. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on my husband's family farm, Marsh Farm, which is four hundred acres of wheat and oilseed, eighty beef cattle and a little farm shop by the road. Mornings I feed and check the cattle with my father-in-law Robert, who's still slow since his stroke, then I open the shop at ten. In between I'm learning the arable side from the contractor, and I've just got my drone licence so I can fly over the crops and spot problems.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a dental receptionist for fifteen years, booking appointments and chasing payments. When Robert had his stroke two years ago, the family needed hands, and my husband Daniel is an electrician with his own customers, so I stepped in on a wage. I'm still the beginner, I had to ask what a heifer was in my first week, but I love it. We've got Leo, who's fourteen, and Maya, who's ten, and our own mortgage on a house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm disappointed, because I'd been looking forward to more. Online I'd say farmers should still use what's there, it saves time. At church I'd say hard work wins, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things carry on, and that's not bad for us. The shop is growing, Daniel's always busy, and we've about four months saved. I'd just keep building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI to write the shop's posts and plan stock. I'd add online orders for beef boxes, which the AI helped me set up last month. And I'd keep learning from the contractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really, things are going well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you used to book appointments. How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I spent fifteen years booking dental appointments, and now an AI app does my farm shop's stock list in five minutes. I use it for the shop's social media, for checking prices, for the drone maps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you about the farm, even in a quiet world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grain prices, the weather, and Robert's health. If something happened to him, the farm decisions would fall to Daniel and me, and we're not ready.

feel: **Calm** and happy, because things are going well.

Sell beef boxes through new online orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, if you're willing to move. At church I'd say God helps those who help themselves. Online I'd share what's working for the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's good for us. The shop ordering, the paperwork, the grant forms, all of it gets easier. The hands-on side is slower, so we've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the shop's ordering and the farm's paperwork this year. I'd look at a small weeding robot with a dealer, to see costs. And I'd put some savings into a better freezer for the beef boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You used to do exactly the kind of work this card says goes first. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I left a reception job just in time, because a computer can now book teeth cleanings better than I ever did. I feel lucky, and a bit sorry for the girls still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should be in charge of how this goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farmers and families, not the government. Too many rules slow things down. Let people try things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say move fast or get left behind. Online I'd tell farmers to get the paperwork sorted now. At church I'd say we need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the shop and paperwork run themselves, fine. But by 2031 the big farms have robots, and beef and grain get cheaper, and we're competing with them. I'm the hands-on worker on our farm, and I'm still learning, so I'd be the one the robot replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd borrow to buy a robot early, through the farm, before prices go up. I'd cut our own spending, no holiday, the second car. And I'd grow the shop, because people still want to meet the farmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like change, but not on someone else's clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years to AGI, robots by 2031. What does that mean on a family farm like Marsh Farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a family farm the robot doesn't take a stranger's job; it takes the job I gave up reception for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leo and Maya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we'll adapt, because Marshes always do. Leo wants to be a pilot, Maya a vet. I'd say keep at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so no excuses. Online I'd share how we're preparing. At church I'd say look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can plan. The paperwork goes by 2031, the hands-on by 2034, and by then Marsh Farm can have robots I chose and run. I'd be the one running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a robot operator course with the dealer next year. I'd save for a robot instead of borrowing. And I'd talk to Daniel's parents about the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. That's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years' warning. Does that change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Get out of the way. Farmers don't need the government to save them; farmers need the government to stop slowing them down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe cheaper loans for small farms. But no handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift. Online I'd say farmers who plan will be fine. At church I'd say the same, plan and pray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'm fine. I'd have time to learn the robots, grow the shop and help run the farm. Daniel's electrician work keeps going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy robots step by step. I'd keep growing the shop. And I'd learn the arable side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years to plan. Is anything still on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only Robert's health, and the family deciding the farm. Not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want Marsh Farm to be by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2039 I want Marsh Farm run by robots I chose, with me in the shop shaking hands with customers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big farms would get robots first and we'd be squeezed. What would help is cheaper loans for small farms and fewer rules. Give a small farm a fair loan and fewer forms, and we'll beat the big ones on our own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: How the customers feel. People still want to buy beef from the person who raised it. That matters.

headlineQuote: Give a small farm a fair loan and fewer forms, and we'll beat the big ones on our own.

She uses **AI daily** for the shop and has a drone licence.
Traditional and **free-market**, she wants fewer rules and no handouts.
She'd **borrow or save** to buy robots early and run them herself.
She's calm in most pictures and **anxious** in AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big robot farms would squeeze Marsh Farm.
